analysis.one_liner: Constitutional amendment letting Congress and states cap campaign spending and require disclosure of political money.
analysis.headline: Bernie Sanders' amendment to reverse the Citizens United decision died in committee with no cosponsors and no committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill proposed amending the Constitution to undo the Citizens United decision. It would say only natural people can spend money to influence elections, and it would spell out that Congress and the states can limit campaign contributions and spending, require disclosure of who is paying, and set up public financing of elections. It explicitly preserves freedom of the press. The bill was read twice in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who want elections decided by citizens rather than by corporate and big-donor spending, candidates without wealthy backers or big-donor access, and small donors whose dollars would count for more under spending limits or public financing.

how_it_helps.text: It would return to Congress and the states the power to limit, cap, and require disclosure of campaign spending that the Supreme Court's Citizens United and related decisions put beyond their reach, restoring limits on corporate and big-donor election spending.

It authorizes public financing of elections so candidates could run without relying on wealthy donors, and requires disclosure of contributions and expenditures so voters can see who is paying for political messages.
It states that elected officials should depend on the people alone, not on private wealth, and preserves freedom of the press so media coverage would not be restricted.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, unions, super PACs, and wealthy individuals who now can spend unlimited amounts on elections would lose that constitutional protection and face limits and disclosure they currently can avoid.

drawbacks.text: Critics argued, in the First Amendment debate the bill itself acknowledges, that capping spending on political messages restricts political speech, and that writing such limits into the Constitution would make them nearly impossible to revise.

The limits would apply to unions as well as corporations, so groups that pool members' money for politics would lose that tool too, which its critics called an unfair restriction on collective speech.

Amending the Constitution requires two-thirds of both chambers plus approval by three-fourths of the states, an extremely high bar, so this route gave the bill almost no realistic chance even with broad public support.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: restoring elected limits on campaign money and opening a public-financing route for candidates without rich backers. The cost is constitutional: spending limits constrain political expression and would be very hard to undo once ratified. The bill was also almost certainly not passable in this form, which makes the practical tradeoff less about design and more about whether its principles ever get a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 12, 2013, proposing a constitutional amendment to reverse the Citizens United decision and let Congress and the states limit money in elections.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.
No senator cosponsored the bill, the committee held no markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, unions, super PACs, and wealthy donors keep the unlimited election-spending rights the Citizens United decision gave them, and officeholders keep a system their critics say ties them to big money. The person who would have benefited most, the voter without big-money backing, is left with the current rules.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the constitutional amendment and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, did not advance the bill to committee action during the 113th Congress.

against.name: Senators who did not cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Chose not to cosponsor the bill, leaving it with zero cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator from either party cosponsored, so the partisan shape of the Senate as a whole was never recorded; the bill's sole sponsor was an Independent.

industries.note: The amendment would end their ability to spend unlimited money on elections and force disclosure of who is funding political messages. Their financial interest in the current system runs directly against voters' interest in seeing where the money comes from.

Citizens United gave corporations a constitutional right to election spending; this amendment would take that away and let Congress and the states cap it. That protection is what the bill's sponsor called the 'corrosive influence' of corporate money on elections.
Like corporations, unions would lose constitutional protection for pooled election spending, so they share the restriction even though some union spending has aimed at goals aligned with workers.
